items.text: – Sure, Baba really hungers for respect. But he ended up with the wrong people; we've smashed every last bit of it.
items.q: Ghassem jokes about their father's need for respect. Does this sound like natural family teasing?
before: Ghassem says:

items.text: – Where on my neck does it say foothold?
items.q: Short-sighted Sajad has stepped on Farid's neck. Does Farid's comeback sound natural?
before: – Ow, ow. Eagle Eye, get your foot off my neck.
– Oh, sorry. Objectively, I'm trying to get to my own bed. It's hard.

items.q: Niloofar teases Amir for listening in on her. Does 'You're very sneaky' sound natural from her?
before: – I heard you talking with a few other girls in the department today.

items.q: Farid asks why both strangers were put in their room. Does Hooman's dry reply sound natural?
before: – With all these rooms with empty beds, why did they send both of them to our room?
Hooman said:

items.text: – Aaawwww. I was the one who told her that. Nini saw it was a good line and passed it on to you.
items.q: Ghassem coos teasingly, revealing that the loving line was his. Does 'Aaawwww' sound natural here?
before: Ghassem says:
– By the way, Amir, when Maman called you a few days ago, did she say, "If you knew how much I love you, you'd be ashamed"?
– Yeah.

items.text: – Everything you do is a patch job.
items.q: Baba is told off for his muddled paperwork. Does 'a patch job' sound natural here?
before: – Look, it can't be done like this: taking the "a" out of the surnames for school and then putting it back again for other offices.
– What's any of this got to do with you? I know what I'm doing.

items.text: A year or two ago I heard from Eagle Eye News that that dandy had gone to Australia too, sort of chasing the girl you both loved.
items.q: Hooman mentions a rich rival. Does 'that dandy' sound natural from a young man today?

items.text: – Haven't you finished what you came for?
items.q: Niloofar wants to end an awkward meeting. Does her line sound natural?
before: – The twenty minutes you said you had are not over yet.
She said:

items.text: – I've loved you for thirty-two months. From a distance. Without your knowing. In silence, without a single word.
items.q: Amir finally declares his love to Niloofar face to face. Does this sound heartfelt and natural?

items.text: – I know. I'm no dummy. But this won't work.
items.q: Niloofar answers Amir, half annoyed. Does 'I'm no dummy' sound natural from her?
before: …and interesting, I can come straight to this bench, sit down, and tell you too. I don't have to wait months on the off chance I'll see you again. How can I put it? A lot of things, if they aren't said then and there, lose their flavor; they go stale. They lose their grace, freshness, and vitality.

items.text: – It makes me so mad when you just sit there in silence like this. I want to punch you.
items.q: Niloofar is exasperated by Amir's silence. Does this sound like her, playful and annoyed?

items.text: – ... I would not take that signet ring of Solomon at any price, for now and then upon it the hand of ...
items.q: Amir reads a broken-off line of Hafez. Does it read as poetry?

items.text: – "For Attar, weeping till dawn is sweeter," or "now he lies more deeply slain"?
items.q: Niloofar asks which song he means by quoting two lines of an Attar poem. Is her question clear?
before: – Want me to send you one track?
– Yes, the one with the Attar verse.

items.text: The light of my dreams ... the light of my dreams turned ... the light of my dreams turned on
items.q: Amir rehearses his love poem, searching for words. Does 'turned on', like a lamp, work in a poem?
before: My dreams were dark
I could see nothing
You came

items.text: Now ... now ... now you are gone ...
items.q: He rehearses the poem, faltering. Does the halting repetition read as poetry, not a mistake?
before: You came
The light of my dreams ... the light of my dreams turned ... the light of my dreams turned on

items.q: This is the opening of Amir's short love poem. Does it read as poetry?
